title: Building a Forward+ Renderer in Rust
description: A look at my OpenGL Forward+ renderer in Rust, focusing on design decisions, abstractions, and how the rendering pipeline works.

content.text: I’ve been working on a renderer/game engine in Rust using OpenGL(calling it acrust for now, as in a pizza crust), and this is one of those projects where I kind of just wanted to see how far I could push myself and learn a little bit about rust.
The main goal was to build a Forward+ renderer from scratch and actually understand what’s happening instead of relying on an engine to abstract everything away.
A big part of that ended up being how I structured my OpenGL code in Rust, which honestly mattered more than I expected.
Why Wrap OpenGL at All?
Raw OpenGL in Rust is… not great. It’s very low-level, very unsafe, and very easy to mess up.
So instead of calling OpenGL directly everywhere, I built small wrappers around core concepts like VAOs, buffers, and attributes.
For example, I have a Vao struct that just owns the OpenGL ID and handles binding:
This isn’t anything fancy, but it already makes the code way more readable and harder to misuse.
Designing Around Rust (Not Fighting It)
One thing I tried to do was not fight Rust’s ownership model. Instead of pretending OpenGL is safe, I just isolated the unsafe parts into small sections.
For example, buffer objects handle their own data uploads:
The idea is: unsafe stays inside the abstraction, and everything else can stay clean.
I also added a small macro to catch OpenGL errors immediately, because debugging silent GL failures is horrible:
Why Forward+?
Traditional forward rendering doesn’t scale well with lots of lights. Every object gets lit by every light, which gets expensive fast.
Deferred rendering solves that, but comes with its own tradeoffs (G-buffer cost, transparency issues, etc.).
Forward+ is kind of a middle ground. You still do forward rendering, but you limit how many lights each fragment considers.
How Forward+ Works (Conceptually)
The idea is to divide the screen into a grid of tiles (for example 16x16 pixel regions).
Then for each tile, you figure out which lights actually affect it.
So instead of every pixel checking every light, each pixel only checks the lights assigned to its tile.
That’s the entire optimization.
Where Depth Comes In
The "plus" in Forward+ usually involves using depth information to make the light culling more accurate.
Instead of just dividing the screen in 2D, you can think of it as slicing space into 3D clusters using depth ranges.
So now lights are assigned not just to screen tiles, but to depth-aware clusters. This avoids lights affecting pixels that are technically in the same tile but far away in depth.
How This Connects to My Design
This is where the buffer abstractions actually matter.
Forward+ relies heavily on GPU-side data structures — things like:

• light lists per tile
• depth data
• cluster indices
In my case, I’m using buffer objects (like SSBOs) to store and pass this data around.
That’s why my BufferObject abstraction supports things like binding to shader storage buffers — it’s not just for vertices anymore.
A Small but Important Detail
One thing I learned pretty quickly is that OpenGL state management is where everything goes wrong.
Binding the wrong buffer, forgetting to unbind something, or accidentally overwriting a binding point can completely break things in ways that are hard to debug.
Wrapping things in structs helped a lot with this, because it forces a more predictable flow.
Final Thoughts
This project has been less about just “making a renderer” and more about understanding how all the pieces actually fit together.
Forward+ has been pretty confusing to understand I will be honest but I now beleive that I have a solid foundation and understand the concepts better than I did when I started.

And honestly, the Rust side of things has been just as interesting and I have learned so much about rust from this project. Figuring out how to structure unsafe OpenGL code in a way that still feels clean and manageable has probably been the most valuable part.

There’s still a lot I want to improve, but this is one of those projects where I actually feel like I understand more than I did when I started — which is kind of the whole point. This project has lot more I could talk about as well. From the ECS System that lends its self well to Rust to the different shaders I used and the terrain generation algorithm that I came up with from this project on my own. But those all deserve their own blog posts wich I will write soon.
